Diagnostic strategy: Age #82

  • (per 100,000 person years)

Notes: first decade –Ewing sarcoma, long bones 10 - 30 yrs – osteosarcoma, Ewing flat bones 30 - 40 yrs - sarcomas > 40 yrs - metastases - multiple myeloma - chondrosarcoma Age is the most important clinical clue in differentiating possible bone tumors. There are many ways of splitting age groups, as can be seen in the table, where  the morphology of a bone lesion is combined with the age of the patient. Some prefer to divide patients into two age groups: younger or older than 30 years. Most primary bone tumors are seen in patients under 30 years. In patients over 30 years we must always include metastases and myeloma in the differential diagnosis.

Benign vs malignant #86

Periosteal reaction (=periostosis) #87

  • Abnormal reaction of the periosteum
  • Frequent in infection and tumor

Notes: Periosteal reaction results when cortical bone reacts to one of many possible insults. Tumor, infection, trauma, certain drugs, and some arthritic conditions can elevate the periosteum from the cortex and form various patterns of periosteal reaction (Fig. 1). Non-aggressive periosteal reactions are slower, with enough time to organize the response. They are often presented as thin, solid, thick, Aggressive periosteal reactions are, however, a consequence of fast bone deposition, in a short period of time, as in malignant tumors or in severe infections, for example; and are often laminated, with onion skin or spiculated,

Hemangioma #94

  • Endothelial tumor – capillary / cavernous
  • Max Frequency: decade 5

  • Location
  • D & L vertebrae
  • Skull (rarely)

Tumors with malignant potential #97

Chondroma #98

  • Mature hyaline cartilage in the medullary cavity
  • 10 % of all benign bone TU
  • 20 – 50 yrs, M = F
  • They grow slowly in childhood and tend to stop at adulthood
  • Location:
  • Small, tubular bones – 50 % hands & feet
  • Humerus, femur

Chondroma #99

  • X-ray
  • Well delineated, mostly lytic (in fingers), lobulated
  • Neighboring cortical - oedostosis

Chondroma #100

  • X-ray
  • Well delineated, mostly sclerotic (in long bones), lobulated
  • Metaphyseal or meta-diaphyseal
  • Neighboring cortical - oedostosis

  • CT:

Chondroma #102

  • MRI:
  • T1 - hypo-/isointense
  • T2 - hyperintense (hyaline cartilage containing water)
  • Peripheral / septal enhancement

Multiple Chondromas (chondromatosis) #103

  • Very rare
  • Ollier syndrome – unilateral (20-30% malignant transformation)
  • Mafucci syndrome – generalized + soft tissue angioamas (>40% malignant transformation)

Chondroma #104

  • Malignant transformation
  • Chondrosarcoma
  • Slow, continuous growth, even after closure of growth plates
  • Follow-up is required

Notes: 2 year interval

Osteochondroma #105

  • Tumor that originates from a misplaced, subperiosteal island of physeal cartilage
  • 45 % of ben bone TU; 12 % of all bone TU
  • 20 – 30 years, M = F
  • Location:
  • metaphyseal, close to epiphysis
  • Multiple = hereditary exostosis

Osteochondroma #106

  • X-ray:
  • =exostosis
  • Pedunculated or sessile
  • Structure similar to bone
  • Cortex continuous to bone

Osteochondroma #107

  • CT:
  • Better outlines contiguity with bone cortex
  • Rarely necessary

MRI: #108

  • Cartilage cap
  • Contiguity with bone marrow
  • Osteochondroma

Osteochondroma #109

  • Malignant transformation:
  • Chondrosarcoma
  • 2 % solitary; 10 % multiple
  • Follow-up required
  • Suspected if it keeps growing after puberty
  • Suspected if thick cartilage cap is present

Multiple myeloma & plasmacytoma #128

  • Malignancy of plasma cells (lymphocytes)
  • Solitary plasmacytoma = tumor cells form a single mass, usually in a bone
  • Multiple myeloma = tumor cells are diffusely spread in the bone marrow
  • The most frequent malignant primary bone tumors
  • Sex: M 2/3 - 3/4 of cases
  • Age: over 40, maximum 6th. decade
  • Location: hematopoietic sites : - vertebrae , ribs , iliac , skull, femur.
  • Lab: 60% Bence Jones proteinuria, 20-50% hypercalcemia, 10 % amyloidosis

SOLITARY PLASMACYTOMA #129

  • X-ray/CT
  • single lesion
  • osteolytic
  • well delineated
  • round /oval
  • no periostosis

  • multiple well-defined "punched out" lytic lesions: predominantly affecting the axial skeleton
  • diffuse skeletal osteopenia
